questions.q: Which iconic building, designed for the 1981 visit of Pope John Paul II, is Mañosa's most famous work and is made almost entirely of materials derived from a single type of tree?
questions.n: Mañosa used every part of the coconut tree—from the trunk to the shell—to prove that local materials are fit for a palace.

questions.q: The San Miguel Corporation Headquarters in Mandaluyong is a landmark of 'Green Architecture.' What natural Philippine landmark inspired its unique, terraced shape?
questions.n: The building's sloping, plant-covered terraces are a direct architectural tribute to the pre-colonial engineering of the Ifugao people.

questions.q: Mañosa designed the world-renowned 'Amanpulo' resort in Palawan. What traditional Filipino dwelling served as the primary inspiration for the guest villas (Casitas)?
questions.n: The casitas mimic the rural nipa hut's pitch, elevation, and openness, but are executed with high-end modern luxuries.

questions.q: The EDSA Shrine (Mary, Queen of Peace) features a unique promenade. What design element did Mañosa use to integrate the church with the busy urban intersection?
o: An underground tunnel that bypasses the street
A giant glass wall to block the noise
A multi-level 'plaza' with steps that allow for mass gatherings and public prayer
questions.n: The design facilitates the role of the site as a space for people to gather, reflecting its history in the People Power Revolution.

questions.q: In his religious works like the Mary Immaculate Parish (Nature Church) in Las Piñas, Mañosa famously used which material for the ceiling to create a 'forest' feel?
o: Thousands of suspended capiz shells and 'anahaw' palm leaves
questions.n: The ceiling uses these organic materials to filter light and sound, making the interior feel like it is sheltered by a canopy of trees.

questions.q: Which specialized structural element did Mañosa often include in his roofs to improve natural ventilation, a hallmark of tropical design?
o: Vented ridges and wide, overhanging eaves
Flat concrete slabs with no openings
questions.n: These features allow hot air to escape from the top while providing shade and protection from heavy tropical rains.

questions.q: Mañosa's design for the 'Pearl Farm Beach Resort' in Samal Island uses roofs that resemble the hats of a specific indigenous group. Which group is it?
o: The Samal and Badjao 'hats' or traditional umbrellas
questions.n: The conical roofs of the resort's guest houses pay homage to the seafaring cultures of the Davao Gulf.

questions.q: True or False: Francisco Mañosa was a staunch critic of the 'International Style' of glass-and-steel boxes, believing they were unsuitable for the Philippine climate.
questions.n: He argued that copying Western skyscrapers led to 'energy-hungry' buildings that ignored the country's natural wind and sun patterns.

questions.q: The 'Moon Garden' and other residential projects by Mañosa often feature the 'Dungon' and 'Guijo' woods. Why did he prefer these specific materials?
o: For their durability, resistance to termites, and natural resonance with the Philippine landscape
Because they are very soft and easy to break
Because they are the cheapest woods available
To make the house look like it's from another country
questions.n: Local hardwoods have evolved to survive the Philippine climate, making them more sustainable for long-term use.

questions.q: Francisco Mañosa was finally conferred the title of National Artist for Architecture in 2018. What was the core reason for this recognition?
o: For his lifelong dedication to the development and promotion of a truly 'Filipino' architecture
For building the tallest building in the world
For his inventions in the field of plastic materials
For his work in designing high-speed railway stations
questions.n: He successfully proved that indigenous forms and materials can be the basis for high-end, contemporary architectural excellence.

questions.q: Francisco Mañosa is famous for using 'Capiz' shells in many of his designs. Besides windows, what is a common way he used this material in his interiors?
o: As decorative light diffusers in chandeliers and ceilings
To create soundproof walls for cinemas
questions.n: The translucent quality of the shell makes it perfect for softening light, creating a warm, traditional Filipino glow.

questions.q: Mañosa often used 'Bamboo' not just for decoration, but as a structural material. What is one major environmental benefit of using bamboo in the Philippines?
o: It is a highly renewable resource that grows locally
It takes hundreds of years to grow, making it rare
It prevents the building from ever catching fire
It is heavier and stronger than solid steel
questions.n: Using local, fast-growing materials like bamboo reduces the carbon footprint and supports local industries.

questions.q: In the 'Coconut Palace,' Mañosa designed columns that look like a specific part of the coconut tree. Which part was it?
questions.n: The columns were designed to mimic the texture and tapering shape of the coconut trunk, literally turning the 'tree of life' into a pillar.

questions.q: True or False: Mañosa believed that a house in the Philippines should be 'breathable' to handle the humidity.
questions.n: His 'Neo-Vernacular' style emphasizes high ceilings and open spaces to allow natural air circulation, just like the traditional Bahay Kubo.

questions.q: The 'Mary Immaculate Parish' (Nature Church) is famous for its roof made of 'Anahaw' leaves. What is 'Anahaw' commonly known as in the Philippines?
questions.n: The large, sturdy leaves of the Anahaw palm are a traditional material for roofing and fans in Filipino culture.

questions.q: Which of these is a key reason why Mañosa used wide 'overhanging eaves' (media agua) in his buildings?
o: To provide a place for people to hide from the police
To reduce the cost of the roof
To protect the walls from heavy rain and direct sunlight
To make the building look like a spaceship
questions.n: In a tropical country, wide eaves keep the interior cool and prevent rain from entering through open windows.

questions.q: Mañosa's design for the LRT-1 stations (the first elevated rail in Southeast Asia) used roofs that looked like what traditional structure?
questions.n: Even for public transport, Mañosa wanted to maintain a Filipino identity by using the familiar pitched-roof silhouette.

questions.q: When Mañosa said 'I design Filipino, nothing else,' what was he encouraging other architects to do?
o: To move all buildings to the province
To find inspiration in local culture and climate instead of just copying the West
To build only with mud and stones
questions.n: He believed that Philippine architecture should be a source of pride and tailored specifically to our unique environment.

questions.q: In the 'Our Lady of Peace' (EDSA) Shrine, the 'Plaza' area is open-air. Why is this important for a Filipino public space?
o: To let the rain wash the floors for free
To allow for large crowds to gather and breathe in a tropical setting
So that people can see the airplanes passing by
Because they ran out of money for a roof
questions.n: Filipino culture is communal; open plazas allow for large groups to meet naturally without the need for expensive air conditioning.

questions.q: Which 'tree' did Mañosa call the 'Tree of Life' because of its 101 uses in his architecture?
questions.n: From the lumber to the shells and the leaves, the coconut provided Mañosa with almost everything he needed to build.
